segments.title: Ernest Appert — 21 Rue Louis-le-Grand
segments.text:
Stop here, outside number twenty-one. Take a good look at this address.

There is nothing here today to suggest that this building played a part in one of the more remarkable chapters of French photographic history.

Yet, in the second half of the nineteenth century, this address was associated with two brothers who took photography far beyond the conventional portrait.

And some of their pictures raise a question we're still asking today.

Can we believe what we see in a photograph?

To understand the brothers' story, we need to go back to the eighteen sixties.

In Paris, photography was becoming a business. Portraits were fashionable. People collected them in albums, exchanged them and gave them to family and friends.

But having your photograph taken was considerably more complicated than pulling a phone out of your pocket.

You had to visit a studio. The lighting had to be carefully controlled. The photographer prepared the plate, the chemicals and the backdrop. And the sitter needed to remain still long enough for a sharp image.

Every portrait called for real skill.

Two brothers worked in this world: Eugène Appert and Ernest-Charles Appert.

They came from Châteauroux, in central France. In Paris, they established themselves among professional photographers, including at this very address, number twenty-one Rue Louis-le-Grand.

Their speciality?

Important people.

Politicians, military officers, judges, aristocrats and public figures.

This was a world in which owning a photograph of a famous person was becoming a way of collecting the news.

Gradually, however, the brothers' work drew closer to something rather different: the world of criminal justice and political upheaval.

Before we come to that, I want to show you an extraordinary little piece of evidence.

A photographic card held by the Rijksmuseum, in Amsterdam, has a kind of advertisement printed on the back.

There are the photographer's professional titles. His claimed distinctions. His associations with prestigious figures.

And his address: number twenty-four, Rue Taitbout.

Then come two more words in French: “Ci-devant”.

Formerly.

The card tells us that the studio had previously been at number twenty-one, Rue Louis-le-Grand.

Even after moving away, the photographer kept the old address on his printed cards.

And here you are, standing directly outside it.

It's a wonderful connection across time.

A tiny line of print, on the back of a photograph, allows us to identify a place that almost nobody would notice as they walked past, more than a hundred and fifty years later.

But what comes next is even more surprising.

The Appert brothers didn't simply photograph people sitting in front of studio backdrops.

They also used a technique that feels remarkably modern: photomontage.

Today, we're familiar with software that can remove a person, change a background or create an entirely imaginary scene.

By the late eighteen sixties, photographers could achieve some of these effects using painstaking manual techniques.

They could assemble portraits. Cut and combine photographic prints. Add drawings or painted details. And then photograph the composite image to create a new print.

Now look at this picture.

Several men appear to be gathered around a table. At first glance, it looks like a scene captured as it happened.

But it is a photomontage.

And that is where the technique becomes fascinating.

A photographer could create the appearance of a meeting that had never been photographed as a meeting.

He could bring different people together into a single composition.

And, crucially, he could lend that constructed scene the apparent authority of a photograph.

People in the nineteenth century did not necessarily have the habits of scepticism that we have developed towards manipulated images.

Then came eighteen seventy.

France went to war with Prussia. The Second Empire collapsed. And Paris approached one of the most violent periods in its history.

In eighteen seventy-one, the Paris Commune erupted. Civil conflict divided the city. There was terrible bloodshed. Hostages were executed. And the suppression of the Commune also cost very many lives.

The Apperts photographed people associated with these events.

But they also produced reconstructed scenes.

One series carried an arresting title: “The Crimes of the Commune”.

Among the events depicted were executions.

And here we need to make a vital distinction.

An event may really have happened.

But a photograph apparently showing that event may have been reconstructed afterwards.

The camera was not necessarily present when it happened.

The figures may have been photographed separately. The setting may have been assembled later.

And yet the finished picture can make you feel as though you're witnessing the very moment of the action.

Take the execution of hostages at La Roquette prison, in May eighteen seventy-one.

The event is part of the history of the Commune.

But Appert's picture is not a photograph taken during the execution.

It is a reconstruction.

And that distinction changes everything.

Imagine someone looking at such a photograph just weeks after the events.

They see a dramatic scene. Victims. Armed men. A setting that seems convincing.

They may believe they're looking at direct evidence.

But what they're looking at is an image composed by a photographer.

This takes us to one of the great questions in the history of the media.

A photograph can be a genuine photographic object, even when the scene it depicts was never photographed in that form.

And there's another dimension to all this.

These pictures circulated in a France deeply divided by politics.

They were not merely technical curiosities.

They could influence how people understood and remembered what had happened. They helped shape a narrative.

Photography was becoming more than a way to preserve history.

It could also be a way of interpreting history.

And sometimes, of steering that interpretation.

Now turn your attention back to the building in front of you.

It might seem that we've simply made an imaginary visit to a nineteenth-century Parisian photography studio.

But the story reaches much further.

At the very moment photography was coming to symbolise truth, some photographers were already learning how to create convincing pictures of reconstructed events.

And there's one final detail worth knowing.

The two brothers often worked under very similar commercial signatures. Archives and catalogues sometimes attribute their photographs differently.

So we must be careful when deciding exactly which work belongs to Eugène and which to Ernest-Charles.

What we can say is that their shared enterprise belongs to the earliest chapters of this extraordinary history of constructed photographic images.

Take one last look at number twenty-one, Rue Louis-le-Grand.

A small Parisian address.

And behind it, an enormous question.

When we look at an image from the past, are we seeing history itself?

Or are we seeing the way somebody chose to show it to us?

Keep that thought in mind.

Our next stop is only a short distance away. And it will take us to a much more recent event.

This time, it won't be a photograph that provides the clue.

It will be a gun.
